parsed.headline: Four killed fighting wildfire in Indonesia’s Bromo Tengger Semeru National Park

pages.text: Four people died on October 15 while attempting to contain a wildfire in the Bromo Tengger Semeru National Park on Java Island, Indonesia. The fire occurred near a savanna and hillside in a crater area, according to reporting from Mongabay. The national park is a complex of active volcanoes and a major tourism destination. Rudijanta Tjahja Nugraha, head of the Bromo Tengger Semeru National Park, stated that officers coordinated with the village government to request personnel assistance to extinguish the fire after receiving notification from the head of Ngadas village. A fire was declared under control on October 14 at approximately 11:45 a.m.

Indonesia’s environment minister identified the four victims as Sukaris, a national park civil servant; Wisnu Yuda Pratama and Sefriel Ardiansyah, employees of the hotel services company PT Mitra Indo Permai; and Hendra Rony Wagiyanta, a member of the state firefighting unit, Manggala Agni. Wagiyanta was evacuated to Tongas hospital in Probolinggo, where he died from injuries hours later. Berton S.P. Panjaitan, a spokesperson for Indonesia’s disaster management agency (BNPB), commented on the victims' dedication to protecting nature and society.

parsed.headline: First Nations leaders report high turnout and voting barriers in Alberta referendum

pages.text: First Nations leaders in Alberta, Canada, have reported high voter turnout during the province's separation referendum, despite allegations of systemic barriers at the ballot box. Jay Telegdi, the Treaty 8 campaign manager, stated that on October 19, 2026, he received numerous calls from individuals reporting they were turned away from voting. Telegdi reported that at least three polling stations on reserves opened late and some locations ran out of ballots early. He also noted reports of voters being denied ballots due to identification issues, specifically regarding the requirement for two pieces of ID when a government-issued photo ID lacks a current physical address, such as when a driver's licence lists a P.O. Box. Telegdi characterized these difficulties as a systemic issue occurring across the province.

In response to reports of ballot shortages, Elections Alberta stated that the shortages indicated higher-than-expected voter turnout among First Nations communities, noting that several locations received multiple ballot deliveries. The agency described the situation as a sign of increased engagement, stating that unofficially, 36 communities participated in 2026 compared to 33 in 2023. While the Siksika Nation chief has sought a formal explanation regarding ballot shortages, Telegdi expressed his belief that the referendum saw the highest Indigenous voter turnout in Alberta's history.

parsed.headline: OCAD University in Toronto to offer 150 scholarships for 150th anniversary

pages.text: OCAD University in Toronto will offer 150 undergraduate scholarships to mark its 150th anniversary, according to the school's president and vice-chancellor, Ana Serrano. The program, named 150 FUTURES, is described by Serrano as the most ambitious scholarship initiative at the institution since its founding in 1876. Each scholarship is valued at $40,000, distributed as $10,000 annually over four years. The scholarships will be available to new student applicants from across Canada who demonstrate financial need, strong academic achievement, and extraordinary creative talent. The university has reported raising more than half of the program's $6-million fundraising goal.

Funding for the scholarship program includes two $1 million gifts from Nancy McCain and Bill Morneau, a former federal finance minister, as well as gifts from John and Jan MacIntyre. John MacIntyre serves as the chair of the TD Bank Group. Originally founded as the Ontario School of Art, the institution was incorporated as the Ontario College of Art in 1912. It changed its name to the Ontario College of Art & Design in 1996 and was granted university status in 2002.

parsed.headline: Yaw Nsarkoh calls for independent prosecutor and questions judicial contempt powers in Ghana

pages.text: Speaking at a JoyNews and An Amalgam of Professionals event in Accra on Tuesday, October 20, 2026, Yaw Nsarkoh, the former Executive Vice President of Unilever Ghana and Nigeria, questioned the use of contempt powers by the judiciary. Mr. Nsarkoh argued that such authority should not be used to discourage legitimate scrutiny of judicial decisions and stated that judicial authority must be subject to critical examination and accountability like any other form of power. He questioned whether contempt proceedings could discourage public criticism of judicial conduct and decisions, raising concerns regarding accountability within the justice system. Mr. Nsarkoh characterized the use of such powers as potentially being a professional irresponsibility if they undermine freedom of speech. He further criticized what he described as performative aggression and hostility within the legal profession and Parliament, questioning why disagreements among public officials often involve shouting and feigned acrimony. Additionally, Mr. Nsarkoh called for the establishment of a muscular, independent prosecutor at the cabinet rank or an equivalent level. He argued this office would strengthen accountability for wrongdoing involving senior political figures, noting that Ghana’s current Attorney-General is appointed by the President and serves as a member of the Cabinet, thereby living in that role at the pleasure of the President.

parsed.headline: EU welcomes Syria’s continued cooperation with chemical weapons watchdog

pages.text: The European Union expressed support for the Organisation for the Prohibition of Chemical Weapons’ (OPCW) work in Syria and welcomed the Syrian authorities’ continued cooperation with the watchdog, according to a statement delivered to the United Nations General Assembly’s First Committee in New York. In the statement, the EU stressed the importance of continued cooperation to resolve outstanding issues regarding the country’s former chemical weapons program. The bloc also welcomed a July 2026 decision by the OPCW Executive Council to reinstate Syria’s rights and privileges under the Chemical Weapons Convention. According to the EU, Syria completed the destruction of Category 3 chemical weapons in August in an operation verified by the OPCW. The EU noted it has supported the OPCW’s work in Syria by providing satellite imagery to strengthen the organization’s operational capabilities. The bloc called for Syria to continue meeting its obligations under the Chemical Weapons Convention to ensure the complete, verified, and irreversible elimination of the chemical weapons program inherited from the former regime. This follows a May 2026 report from the OPCW stating that an expert team deployed to Syria discovered previously undeclared chemical weapons, documentation, and related materials with the support of Syrian authorities. The OPCW continues to work with Syrian authorities to address outstanding issues under the framework of the Chemical Weapons Convention.

parsed.headline: Ghanaian Minister calls for strengthened science journalism to bridge research-industry gap

pages.text: Dr. Zanetor Agyeman-Rawlings, Ghana's Minister of Environment, Science and Technology, stated that journalists must strengthen science reporting to bridge the gap between research institutions, industry, and the public. Speaking at the closing ceremony of the 2026 UK Media Excellence for Emerging Technologies (UK MEET) Fellowship in Accra, the Minister noted that journalists play a role in translating scientific discoveries and technological innovations into information usable by businesses, policymakers, and citizens. Dr. Agyeman-Rawlings said that while researchers often focus on developing knowledge, they require effective communication and commercialization support to connect their work to industry and the wider public. She suggested that science journalism could draw attention to locally developed solutions, encourage collaboration between researchers and businesses, and ensure research contributes to national development. The Minister urged reporters to follow up on whether innovations are adopted or commercialized rather than reporting discoveries as isolated events, and to explain both the benefits and potential risks of emerging technologies.

Professor Eric Opoku Mensah, Vice-Chancellor of the University of Media, Arts and Communication (UniMAC), added that journalists need to bring research and innovation from laboratories and academic institutions into everyday public conversations. Discussing the media's role in West Africa’s science and innovation story, Professor Opoku Mensah urged reporters to examine the evidence behind scientific claims, including study conduct, replication, and remaining uncertainties. He cautioned against presenting preliminary findings as established facts or describing promising treatments as cures without sufficient evidence. Professor Opoku Mensah also recommended that journalists explain technical concepts in accessible language, use local languages where appropriate, and seek the views of individuals affected by scientific and technological developments.

parsed.headline: Bangladesh climate finance agenda focuses on debt service and human capital costs

pages.text: Syed Nasim Manzur, writing for The Financial Express Bangladesh, argues that Bangladesh’s climate finance agenda at the upcoming COP31 should prioritize the distinction between an investment's societal value and the cash available to service its debt. Manzur, who is preparing to travel with a Monash University delegation to COP31 in Antalya, Türkiye, notes that while infrastructure like embankments can prevent enormous losses, such assets may not generate the revenue required to repay the loans used to build them. This perspective follows recent Pre-COP31 meetings in Fiji, where Pacific representatives stated that countries facing rising climate costs cannot borrow their way out of every threat. Manzur suggests that Bangladesh should evaluate financing offers based on terms, arrival timing, and risk distribution, noting that a grant and a loan of the same face value are not equivalent. The discussion of climate-related losses extends to human capital; UNICEF reported that extreme weather disrupted the schooling of 35 million children in Bangladesh in 2024.
